catalog_quote: 形態標示をおこなわない，いわゆる孤立語的性格の強いパラウク・ワ語においては，純粋に形態論的観点から，語と句を区別することができない。また，弁別特徴としての語アクセントをもたないため，音韻的にこれを判別することも困難である。例えば，休止により規定される多音節の音韻領域であれば，どのような統語単位であれ，同じような卓立（強さ）を観察することができる。以下，音節を単位とする相対的な強さ・弱さをそれぞれ●，○と表す。(5) pauʔʔac （○●）「兄弟」 (6) ɲɛʔsioʔsiɔ （○○●）「学校」 (7) ruŋ krak （○●）「水牛の角」 (8) ruŋ krak yum （○○●）「死んだ水牛の角」 (9) ruŋ krak yum kiʔ （○○○●）「彼（女）たちの死んだ水牛の角」 (5)(6)は語であり，(7)から(9)は句である。いずれも最終音節に卓立が現れるため，音調パターンによって単位を同定することは不可能である。つまり，パラウク・ワ語における語と句の区別は，もっぱら統語的観点（一部構成要素のみに統語操作が可能か否か）からなされるということになる。... (10) haukhuan （○●） （< + ） 発展する 上る 膨らむ (11) {lih jɯ} {hauk blauŋ} （○●○●） 「うろうろする。」 (10)のような類似並列語では，卓立が唯一の音韻領域の末尾に現れる。一方，(11)のような類似並列句においては，並列要素間に若干の音声的休止が観察されるため，全体として二つの音韻領域が認められる。 [Yamada 2016: 13-14] そもそも、「副音節」は多音節語における弱化現象として分析されるものであり、本質的に形態法とは別次元の問題と考えるべきである。例えば次の（5）は明らかな複合語であるが、パラウク・ワ語の固定的なアクセントパターン（弱‐強）に従うかたちで、前部音節が弱化して実現されることがある。(5) maoʔkhlaʔ 〜 makhlaʔ 「ベルト」（＜ maoʔ「紐」、khlaʔ「ズボン」）

new_statements.translation: Moreover, since [Parauk Wa] has no word accent as a distinctive feature, it is also difficult to make this distinction [word vs. phrase] phonologically. For example, in any polysyllabic phonological domain delimited by pauses, whatever the syntactic unit, the same kind of prominence (strength) can be observed. Below, relative strength and weakness per syllable are shown as ● and ○. (5) pauʔʔac (○●) 'brothers' (6) ɲɛʔsioʔsiɔ (○○●) 'school' (7) ruŋ krak (○●) 'buffalo horn' (8) ruŋ krak yum (○○●) 'horn of the dead buffalo' (9) ruŋ krak yum kiʔ (○○○●) 'the horn of their dead buffalo'. (5)-(6) are words and (7)-(9) are phrases. Since prominence appears on the final syllable in every case, it is impossible to identify the unit from its prosodic pattern. [Supporting, Yamada 2016: 13-14: '… realized with the first syllable weakened, in accordance with Parauk Wa's fixed accent pattern (weak-strong)'.]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Prominence falls on the last syllable of any pause-delimited polysyllabic unit; all preceding syllables are weak (○○●). Yamada 2016 calls this the language's 'fixed accent pattern (weak-strong)' and derives the minor (pre-)syllable from weakening of the non-final syllable of polysyllables/compounds (maoʔkhlaʔ ~ makhlaʔ 'belt'). Word accent is not contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; every non-final syllable is marked weak, including in three- and four-syllable units.
new_statements.exceptions: None to the placement rule. Yamada 2016: 18 notes emphatic reduplications (cɯiʔcɯiʔ ~ cɯicɯiʔ 'a little') carry a distinctive [554.21] pitch intonation; Watkins 2002: 171 notes an emphatic long high tone on utterance-final syllables / 'any stressed word' in narrative style.
new_statements.domain_note: The prominence unit is the pause-bounded phonological domain, which can be a word or a phrase — the author's point is that word and phrase show the identical final-prominence pattern, so word accent is not a distinctive feature. Words in the examples are polysyllabic (compound/sesquisyllabic) citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Yamada's 'Parauk Wa' (パラウク・ワ語) = Parauk/Paraok, ISO prk = para1301; data collected in Cangyuan county (滄源県) and Kunming, Yunnan, i.e. the Chinese side of the Standard/PRC Wa continuum, not the Burmese Bible-Wa standard described by Watkins 2002. Same Glottolog languoid; no dialect glottocode needed. The Wikipedia 'final-syllable stress' line concerns Lavïa (a different Palaungic language, Sun 2018b) and is not evidence for para1301.

new_statements.quote: [p. 63] The phonological word in Wa of Ban Santisuk Moo 19 has only one main (strong) stress. That is, a strong stressed syllable shows the end of a phonological word. Thus a phonological word in this study may be called a stress group as well. [pp. 65-66] The stress group in Wa at Ban Santisuk Moo 19 has only one strong stress on the peak of the monosyllabic word and on the last syllable of the disyllabic and trisyllabic words. And also, there are the weak stress on the minor syllable or the unstress on the presyllable and the nasal syllable that can occur everywhere except the end of words in the disyllabic and trisyllabic word. Stress in Wa at Ban Santisuk Moo 19 is predictable; therefore, it is not marked in phonemic writing.

Thus a phonological word in this study may be called a stress group as well.'; printed p. 65 (end of §5.2.3) reads exactly 'The stress group in Wa at Ban Santisuk Moo 19 has only one strong stress on the peak of the monosyllabic word and on the last syllable of the disyllabic and trisyllab…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (final-syllable stress, final stress) and as Yamada 2010/2016 (fixed weak-strong, final prominence, non-distinctive); adds an explicit three-degree stress scale (weak stress on non-final full syllables, unstressed presyllables and nasal syllables), the statement that stress is predictable/unmarked phonemically, the domain (phonological word = stress group, strong stress marks the word's end), and non-contrastive word pitch. Caveat on identity: the variety is the Wa of migrants from the Wa States of Burma settled c. 1982 at Ban Santisuk Moo 19, Mae Chan, Chiang Rai (Thailand); the author does not assign it to Parauk or any named Wa dialect.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every phonological word (= stress group) carries exactly one strong stress, on its final syllable (the 'major syllable', whose occurrence is obligatory in final position); mono-, di- and trisyllabic words are all stressed on the last syllable; stress is predictable and non-contrastive. The abstract restates it: 'Each word-type must be stressed strongly on the final syllable of word.' (p. iv). Word pitch (low, mid, high-falling, high) is likewise non-contrastive, conditioned by the vowel and final consonant (§5.3, p. 66).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three degrees: strong ['] on the final major syllable; weak [,] on 'minor syllables' (full-vowel non-final syllables: the penult of disyllabic sub-type B [ˌw's], the first or second syllable of trisyllables [ˌw u 's], [u ˌw 's]); presyllables [Cə]/[Ca] and syllabic-nasal syllables are unstressed (§4.2.2-4.2.4, §4.3.2, §5.2).
new_statements.exceptions: None; stress is stated to be fully predictable. Trisyllabic words are very few (five in the data). Presyllable vowel /ə/~/a/ in free variation.
new_statements.identity_note: Watkins 2019 describes the standard Paraok of Aishuai/Yanshuai (Cangyuan county, Yunnan). Wattana 1998 describes the Wa spoken by c. 28 households of migrants from several villages of the Wa States of Burma (informants from a village scanned-read as 'paŋkʰriam'), settled c. 1982 at Ban Santisuk Moo 19, Tambol Patung, Mae Chan district, Chiang Rai, Thailand; autonym scanned-garbled (/ʔavɯaʔ/-like); the thesis never names the dialect as Parauk (27 consonants, no register contrast reported, final /-s/ retained), so its filing under para1301 rests on the catalog/Glottolog assignment, not on the author. Yamada's statements already held by the project are from Cangyuan/Kunming Parauk; Ma Seng Mai 2012 (held by the project, silent) is Yaong Soi (Bible Wa) in Shan State.

sources.note: Secondary. Standard Wa described as non-tonal with tense/lax register, syllable C(C)(V)V(V)(C); no stress statement for Parauk. The 'stress falls at the final syllables … preceded by an unstressed minor syllable' line is for Lavïa (a different Palaungic variety, after Sun 2018b), not South Wa.

sources.note: pp. 13-14: minor ('副') syllables are weakened first syllables of polysyllables, e.g. maoʔkhlaʔ ~ makhlaʔ 'belt', 'in accordance with Parauk Wa's fixed accent pattern (weak-strong)' (パラウク・ワ語の固定的なアクセントパターン（弱‐強）). Emphatic reduplications carry a special [554.21] pitch intonation (p. 18).

sources.note: §3 (p. 5): Parauk Wa has no word accent as a distinctive feature; in any pause-delimited polysyllabic domain, word or phrase alike, the same prominence (strength) appears on the FINAL syllable (○●, ○○●, ○○○●), so word and phrase cannot be told apart prosodically. Data from the author's fieldwork in Cangyuan county and Kunming, Yunnan (p. 15).
